title: Long Waiting Times at Accident and Emergency Departments of Restructured Hospitals
what_it_is: Long Waiting Times at Accident and Emergency Departments of Restructured Hospitals

sections.label: Hospital waiting time questions
sections.summary: Questions ask the Minister for Health about reducing A&E and ward waiting times, bed crunch causes, elective surgery postponements and bed space solutions.

sentences.speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
sentences.text: asked the Minister for Health (a) what is being done to reduce the waiting time for (i) consultation at the accident and emergency departments of public hospitals and (ii) ward beds at public hospitals; (b) whether the waiting time has reduced; and (c) if so, by how much.

sentences.speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
sentences.text: asked the Minister for Health (a) whether an in-depth analysis is being done to identify the underlying causes of the hospital bed crunch problem; (b) how will hospitals ensure that care for patients in holding spaces, including those with non-critical issues, will not be compromised; (c) what mechanism is in place for the different healthcare clusters to forecast and raise the alarm about possible upward demand at emergency departments to make necessary arrangements in advance; and (d) when is the bed crunch expected to ease.

sentences.speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
sentences.text: asked the Minister for Health (a) what are the main reasons behind the long waiting times for admission at some restructured hospitals' emergency departments in recent weeks; and (b) what are the measures the Ministry is taking to reduce waiting time especially for patients with higher acuity conditions.

sentences.speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
sentences.text: asked the Minister for Health in light of the current hospital bed crunch (a) whether non-urgent elective surgeries in public hospitals will be postponed; (b) if so, whether this will once more result in a backlog after the current bed crunch is alleviated; and (c) how will the Ministry prevent the occurrences of deferring non-urgent treatments from turning into a vicious cycle of care backlog.

sentences.speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
sentences.text: asked the Minister for Health (a) what are the critical bottlenecks in hospitals resulting in patients being held for long periods of time at emergency departments; (b) whether this has resulted in ambulances being unable to be deployed for other emergencies; and (c) what steps is the Ministry taking to more permanently resolve the lack of bed spaces in public hospitals.

sections.label: Emergency department waiting times
sections.summary: Median ED consultation waits averaged about 20 minutes and ward waits about seven hours from January to September, spiking to 50 hours in busier hospitals.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: For non-life-threatening but emergency cases, the median waiting times for consultation across all our EDs are averaged to about 20 minutes from January to September this year.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: For emergency cases that require hospital admission – this is where the bottleneck is – the median waiting times for wards is about seven hours, from January to September.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: It is a few hours longer than 2019.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: What I quoted, "seven hours", that is the median.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: So, when we have an infection wave, like recently, waiting times can spike up sharply – to the reported 50 hours – for certain hospitals that are busier.

sections.label: Unsustainable current situation
sections.summary: The current situation is not sustainable and needs to be resolved.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: The current situation, make no mistake, is not sustainable, and we need to resolve it.

sections.label: Falling monthly ED attendances
sections.summary: Average monthly ED attendances fell from 75,000 patients in 2019 to 63,000 patients in 2022.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: If we look at average monthly ED attendances, which translate into demand for hospital beds – from 2019, before COVID-19 started – to 2022, there is a reduction from 75,000 patients per month to 63,000 patients per month.

sections.label: Rising share of high-acuity patients
sections.summary: The proportion of highest-acuity ED patients rose from about 8% in 2019 to 11% in 2022.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: Or there can be a simple reason – that during a pandemic, people actually do not like to go to EDs; that is also a possible reason.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: However, while the overall number dropped, if you look at all ED attendances, the proportion of patients with highest acuity – this means they have the most serious conditions and need the most attention and probably need hospital beds – had increased from about 8% in 2019 to 11% in 2022.

sections.label: COVID-19 added ED visits
sections.summary: At the mid-year Omicron and recent XBB peaks, COVID-19 infected patients added another 600 ED visits every day.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: For example, at the peak of the mid-year Omicron wave and the recent XBB wave, COVID-19 infected patients added another 600 ED visits every day.

sections.label: Longer hospital stays doubled
sections.summary: Patients staying longer than 21 days doubled from 1.6% of hospitalised patients in 2019 to 3.8% in 2022.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: To illustrate, the percentage of patients who stay longer than 21 days has doubled from 1.6% of all hospitalised patients in 2019 to 3.8% in 2022.

sections.label: Flexible ringfenced bed numbers
sections.summary: The number of ringfenced beds is raised or lowered with the pandemic situation, such as 800 beds during the XBB wave peak.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: However, we inject flexibility into the plan, raising or lowering the number of ringfenced beds according to the pandemic situation.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: So, for example, again, at the peak of the recent XBB wave, we set aside 800 beds for COVID-19 patients, as ringfence.

sections.label: More hospital beds and TCFs
sections.summary: Over five years about 1,900 more public hospital beds are targeted, and three Transitional Care Facilities with 400 beds are already operating.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: Over the next five years, we target to add about 1,900 more public hospital beds, including the aforementioned two projects, and also the expanded Singapore General Hospital Medical Campus.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: Number one, we will activate more TCFs, what we call Transitional Care Facilities.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: Three TCFs are already in operation, with a total of 400 beds.

sections.label: Move away from ringfencing beds
sections.summary: A more flexible and balanced approach to hospital bed assignments is needed, moving away from ringfencing beds just for COVID-19 patients.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: It is time for us adopt a more flexible and balanced approach to hospital bed assignments.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: We should move away from ringfencing beds just for COVID-19 patients.

sections.label: Non-urgent ED attendances share
sections.summary: ED attendances have fallen compared to 2019, but non-urgent cases still make up 40% of all ED attendances.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: While ED attendances have fallen compared to 2019, non-urgent cases still make up 40% of all ED attendances.

sections.label: Vaccination and hospital beds
sections.summary: Seniors without minimum vaccination protection are about three times more likely to be hospitalised, so another jab may free up a hospital bed.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: Today, a senior without minimum vaccination protection is still about three times more likely to end up in hospital and needing to be warded, than one with minimum vaccination protection.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: So, by taking another jab to keep vaccination up-to-date, you may well be freeing up an additional hospital bed.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: If we can do our part, we will help healthcare workers earn back their normalcy of life, as they have sacrificed and worked hard to earn our freedom and normalcy of life.

sections.label: Postponed procedures backlog clearance
sections.summary: The recent wave postponed only 5% to 10% of procedures, not a huge backlog, to be cleared as soon as possible.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: In the recent wave, we postponed some, but only 5% to 10%.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: So, it is not a huge backlog and certainly we will want to clear it as soon as possible.

sections.label: TCF costs and beds freed
sections.summary: TCFs cost no different from public hospitals, and at least 200 to 300 beds could be freed up.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: Two, TCFs cost no different from public hospitals.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: And finally, the percentage, or number of beds that would be freed up, I gave a ballpark just now at the peak of the Omicron variant XBB wave, we were still setting aside 160 beds at the peak; sterilised it, ringfenced it, even though we had patients waiting downstairs because we were afraid of a spike of COVID-19 patients.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: So, I would say, at least 200 to 300 beds.

sections.label: Short-term recruitment and training
sections.summary: This can be solved in the short term over a few months by recruiting, training and putting them in place.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: Fortunately, this is something we can solve in the short term, over a few months, by recruiting, training them and putting them in place.

sections.label: GPFirst clinics at Changi
sections.summary: GPFirst was piloted at Changi General Hospital in 2014, and the question asks how many of about 1,800 GP clinics are on it.

sentences.speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: Pertaining to the GPFirst initiative that was piloted in Changi General Hospital back in 2014, how many of our current slate of about 1,800 GP clinics are on it?

sections.label: Call line to EDs
sections.summary: Calling EDs adds to their workload, but AIC can be approached to help link up with the nearest EDs.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: As to whether to set up a call line to EDs, I suppose the more they call, it does add to the workload of EDs as well.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: Notwithstanding that, I think we can approach the Agency for Intergrated Care (AIC), and AIC will help link up with the nearest EDs.

sections.label: TCFs and urgent care centres
sections.summary: A TCF is not quite the place to refer ED cases to, and more Urgent Care Centres are being set up.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: A TCF is not quite the place to refer ED cases to.

sentences.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
sentences.text: But what we are doing is setting up more Urgent Care Centres (UCCs).
